abandon.simpleDefinition: To leave a place, person, or thing permanently, especially when you should stay.
abandon.example: The crew had to abandon the sinking ship.

abate.simpleDefinition: To become less intense or widespread, or to make something less intense.
abate.example: The storm finally began to abate after hours of heavy rain.

abatement.simpleDefinition: The process of reducing or making something less intense or severe.
abatement.example: The city council approved a tax abatement for new businesses.

abeyance.simpleDefinition: A state of temporary disuse or suspension.
abeyance.example: The project was held in abeyance until funding could be secured.

abhorrence.simpleDefinition: A feeling of intense disgust and hatred.
abhorrence.example: She felt an intense abhorrence for violence of any kind.

abolish.simpleDefinition: To formally put an end to a system, practice, or institution.
abolish.example: Many countries have worked to abolish the death penalty.

above board.simpleDefinition: Open, honest, and legitimate, without any secrecy or deception.
above board.example: All their business dealings were completely above board.

abrasive.simpleDefinition: Causing irritation or annoyance; also, capable of polishing or cleaning a hard surface by rubbing or grinding.
abrasive.example: His abrasive comments often offended people, even when he didn't mean to.

abscond.simpleDefinition: To leave secretly and suddenly, often to avoid arrest or punishment.
abscond.example: The suspect absconded with the stolen money before the police arrived.

abstinent.simpleDefinition: Choosing not to do something, especially not to drink alcohol or engage in certain pleasures.
abstinent.example: She remained abstinent from sugar for a month as part of her diet.

abundance.simpleDefinition: A very large quantity of something; plentifulness.
abundance.example: The region enjoys an abundance of natural resources.

abuse.simpleDefinition: The improper, harmful, or cruel treatment of a person, animal, or thing.
abuse.example: The charity works to prevent child abuse and neglect.

abyss.simpleDefinition: A deep or seemingly bottomless chasm or pit.
abyss.example: The climbers looked down into the dark abyss below them.

accidental.simpleDefinition: Happening by chance or unexpectedly, without being planned or intended.
accidental.example: The spilled coffee was a purely accidental mishap.

accretion.simpleDefinition: The process of growth or increase by gradual accumulation of additional layers or matter.
accretion.example: The island grew larger over time due to the accretion of sand and sediment.

accrue.simpleDefinition: To accumulate or receive something, especially payments or benefits, over time.
accrue.example: Interest will accrue on the savings account over the next year.

accumulate.simpleDefinition: To gather or acquire an increasing number or quantity of something over a period of time.
accumulate.example: Dust began to accumulate on the old furniture in the empty house.

accuse.simpleDefinition: To charge someone with an offense or crime.
accuse.example: The police accused him of theft after finding the stolen goods in his car.

acquit.simpleDefinition: To free someone from a criminal charge by a verdict of not guilty.
acquit.example: The jury decided to acquit the defendant due to lack of evidence.

acrimonious.simpleDefinition: (Typically of a speech or debate) angry and bitter.
acrimonious.example: Their divorce was marked by a series of acrimonious arguments over property.

adamant.simpleDefinition: Refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind.
adamant.example: She was adamant that she would not change her decision.

adapt.simpleDefinition: To adjust to new conditions or to make something suitable for a new use or purpose.
adapt.example: It took some time for the new employees to adapt to the company culture.

adequacy.simpleDefinition: The state or quality of being enough or suitable for a particular purpose.
adequacy.example: They questioned the adequacy of the safety measures in place.

adequate.simpleDefinition: Enough or satisfactory for a particular purpose.
adequate.example: The small budget was barely adequate for the project's needs.

admits.simpleDefinition: To confess to be true or to allow someone to enter a place.
admits.example: The suspect finally admits his involvement in the crime.

adopt.simpleDefinition: To legally take another person's child into your family and raise them as your own, or to choose to take up or follow an idea, plan, or method.
adopt.example: The city council decided to adopt a new policy to improve public transportation.

adopted.simpleDefinition: Having been legally taken into another family to be raised as their child, or having been chosen and taken up as a new idea or method.
adopted.example: The adopted child quickly felt at home with her new parents.

adoring.simpleDefinition: Showing deep love, admiration, or worship for someone or something.
adoring.example: The adoring fans cheered loudly when their favorite band appeared on stage.

adornment.simpleDefinition: Something that is used to decorate or make something more attractive.
adornment.example: The ancient queen wore elaborate gold adornments on her hair and clothing.

adverse.simpleDefinition: Causing problems or difficulties; unfavorable or harmful.
adverse.example: The team faced adverse weather conditions during their mountain climb.

affirm.simpleDefinition: To state something as true or to show a strong belief in something.
affirm.example: She affirmed her commitment to the project by working extra hours.

aftermath.simpleDefinition: The consequences or results of an unpleasant event, especially a disaster or accident.
aftermath.example: The city struggled to rebuild in the aftermath of the devastating earthquake.

agile.simpleDefinition: Able to move quickly and easily, or able to think and understand quickly.
agile.example: The agile gymnast performed a series of impressive flips and twists.

agitation.simpleDefinition: A state of anxiety or nervous excitement, or the act of stirring or shaking something.
agitation.example: There was considerable public agitation over the proposed new tax.

agnostic.simpleDefinition: A person who believes that it is impossible to know whether God exists or not.
agnostic.example: As an agnostic, he was open to different spiritual ideas but didn't claim to know the ultimate truth.

ailment.simpleDefinition: A minor illness or sickness, often one that is not very serious.
ailment.example: She visited the doctor for a common ailment, a persistent cough.

alabaster.simpleDefinition: A soft, white, translucent stone, often used for carving ornaments or statues.
alabaster.example: The sculptor carved a delicate figure from a block of alabaster.

alienation.simpleDefinition: The feeling of being isolated or separated from a group, society, or one's own feelings.
alienation.example: The new employee felt a sense of alienation from her colleagues because of their different interests.

allay.simpleDefinition: To make a strong feeling, such as fear, concern, or suspicion, less intense or severe.
allay.example: The doctor tried to allay the patient's fears about the upcoming surgery.

alluring.example: The alluring scent of freshly baked bread drew customers into the bakery.

amalgamate.simpleDefinition: To combine or unite to form one larger organization or structure.
amalgamate.example: The two small companies decided to amalgamate to create a stronger business.

amass.simpleDefinition: To gather or collect a large amount of something, especially money or information, over a period of time.
amass.example: She managed to amass a considerable fortune through shrewd investments.

amateur.simpleDefinition: A person who engages in an activity for pleasure rather than for financial gain or professional reasons.
amateur.example: He was an amateur photographer, but his pictures were often stunning.

ambidextrous.simpleDefinition: Able to use both the right and left hands equally well.
ambidextrous.example: The ambidextrous artist could draw intricate details with either hand.

ameliorate.simpleDefinition: To make something bad or unsatisfactory better or more tolerable.
ameliorate.example: Efforts were made to ameliorate the harsh living conditions in the refugee camp.

amenable.simpleDefinition: Willing to accept or be influenced by a suggestion, or easily controlled.
amenable.example: The team leader was amenable to suggestions for improving the project workflow.

amicable person.simpleDefinition: Characterized by friendliness and good will, especially between people or groups.
amicable person.example: Despite their disagreements, they managed to reach an amicable settlement.

amity.simpleDefinition: A friendly relationship, especially between countries or groups.
amity.example: The two nations worked to foster amity after years of tension.

amplification.simpleDefinition: The process of making something larger, stronger, or more intense, especially sound, or providing more details about something.
amplification.example: The concert hall required sound amplification so that everyone could hear the music clearly.

ancillary.simpleDefinition: Providing necessary support to the primary activities or operation of an organization, system, or process.
ancillary.example: The company provides ancillary services like cleaning and security for its main clients.

anemometer.simpleDefinition: A device used to measure the speed of the wind.
anemometer.example: The weather station installed a new anemometer to get more accurate wind readings.

animate.example: Children often imagine their toys are animate and talk to them.

annul.simpleDefinition: To declare something, like a law or marriage, no longer valid or legally binding.
annul.example: The court decided to annul the contract due to a technical error.

anomalous.simpleDefinition: Different from what is normal, expected, or standard; unusual.
anomalous.example: The scientist observed an anomalous reading on the instrument, which required further investigation.

anonymous.simpleDefinition: Not identified by name; unknown or unnamed.
anonymous.example: An anonymous donor contributed a large sum of money to the charity.

antagonism.simpleDefinition: Active hostility or opposition between two people or groups.
antagonism.example: There was a strong antagonism between the rival teams before the championship game.

anticipated.simpleDefinition: Expected or predicted something to happen; looked forward to.
anticipated.example: Everyone anticipated the arrival of the new product with great excitement.

apathetic.simpleDefinition: Showing or feeling no interest, enthusiasm, or concern.
apathetic.example: The students became apathetic about the lesson because the teacher made it very boring.

aphorism.simpleDefinition: A short, clever saying that expresses a general truth or principle.
aphorism.example: "Actions speak louder than words" is a well-known aphorism.

appall.simpleDefinition: To greatly shock or horrify someone.
appall.example: The news of the natural disaster appalled people around the world.

apparent.example: It was apparent from her expression that she was unhappy with the decision.

appeal.simpleDefinition: A serious or urgent request for something, often help or support.
appeal.example: The charity launched an appeal for donations to help the flood victims.

applaud.simpleDefinition: To show approval or praise by clapping hands or shouting.
applaud.example: The audience began to applaud loudly after the amazing performance.

applause.simpleDefinition: The sound of people clapping their hands to show approval or praise.
applause.example: The actor received a standing ovation and thunderous applause at the end of the play.

appraisal.simpleDefinition: An act of assessing the value, quality, or performance of something or someone.
appraisal.example: The annual appraisal helps employees understand their strengths and areas for improvement.

arbitrary.simpleDefinition: Based on random choice or personal whim, rather than any reason or system.
arbitrary.example: The judge's decision seemed arbitrary, as it wasn't based on any clear legal precedent.

archives.simpleDefinition: A collection of historical documents or records providing information about a place, institution, or group of people.
archives.example: Researchers spent hours in the city archives looking for old maps and historical letters.

arduous.simpleDefinition: Involving or requiring strenuous effort; difficult and tiring.
arduous.example: Climbing to the summit of the mountain was an arduous task.

argument.simpleDefinition: A reason or set of reasons given with the aim of persuading others that an action or idea is right or wrong. Also, a disagreement.
argument.example: The lawyers presented their arguments to the jury.

argumentative.simpleDefinition: Tending to argue or disagree; fond of arguing.
argumentative.example: He was known for his argumentative nature, always ready to challenge someone's opinion.

aristocrat.simpleDefinition: A person belonging to the highest class in certain societies, often with special social or political status.
aristocrat.example: The old aristocrat lived in a grand mansion with many servants.

arouse.simpleDefinition: To awaken a feeling, emotion, or response; to stir up.
arouse.example: The speaker's powerful words aroused strong emotions in the audience.

arrogant.simpleDefinition: Having or revealing an exaggerated sense of one's own importance or abilities.
arrogant.example: His arrogant attitude made it difficult for him to work well with others.

artillery.simpleDefinition: Large-caliber guns used in warfare, such as cannons, or the branch of an army that uses them.
artillery.example: The army used heavy artillery to defend their position against the enemy attack.

artistic.simpleDefinition: Relating to art or artists; having or showing creative skill.
artistic.example: She has a very artistic eye and can turn everyday objects into beautiful decorations.

ascend.simpleDefinition: To move upwards or climb to a higher position.
ascend.example: The hikers began to ascend the steep mountain path at dawn.

assert.simpleDefinition: To state something confidently and forcefully, or to behave in a way that shows you have power.
assert.example: She needed to assert her authority in the meeting to get her point across.

assiduous.simpleDefinition: Showing great care, attention, and effort in one's work or duties.
assiduous.example: The assiduous student spent hours in the library preparing for the exam.

asylum.simpleDefinition: Protection or safety given by a government to someone who has left their own country because they are in danger. It can also mean a place of refuge.
asylum.example: Many people seek political asylum in other countries to escape persecution.

at bottom.simpleDefinition: Used to say what is the true or fundamental nature of something or someone, despite appearances.
at bottom.example: He seems gruff, but at bottom, he's a very kind and compassionate person.

attempts.simpleDefinition: Efforts made to achieve or do something.
attempts.example: Despite several attempts, they couldn't solve the complex puzzle.

attribute.simpleDefinition: To regard something as being caused by or belonging to someone or something.
attribute.example: She attributed her success to hard work and dedication.

audacity.simpleDefinition: The willingness to take bold risks, or rude or disrespectful behavior.
audacity.example: He had the audacity to ask for a raise after being late every day for a month.

autocrat.simpleDefinition: A ruler who has absolute power and makes decisions without consulting anyone else.
autocrat.example: The country was governed by an autocrat who tolerated no dissent.

aversion.simpleDefinition: A strong feeling of dislike or opposition towards something.
aversion.example: She had a strong aversion to public speaking, always feeling nervous before presentations.

awkward.simpleDefinition: Difficult to use or handle; causing embarrassment or discomfort.
awkward.example: There was an awkward silence after he made the inappropriate comment.

axle.simpleDefinition: A rod or spindle (either fixed or rotating) passing through the center of a wheel or group of wheels.
axle.example: The car's axle broke, leaving it stranded on the side of the road.

backtrack.simpleDefinition: To go back along the same path one has just taken, or to withdraw from a position or statement previously made.
backtrack.example: After realizing his mistake, he had to backtrack on his earlier statement.

bait.simpleDefinition: Food or other enticement used to attract fish or other animals, or something used to tempt someone to do something.
bait.example: The detective used a fake diamond as bait to catch the thief.

ball to the wall.simpleDefinition: To do something with maximum effort, speed, or intensity.
ball to the wall.example: With only an hour left, they went ball to the wall to finish the project on time.

balmy.simpleDefinition: (Of weather) pleasantly warm and mild; also, slightly crazy or foolish.
balmy.example: We enjoyed a balmy evening stroll along the beach.

bankrupt.simpleDefinition: Unable to pay one's debts; legally declared to be financially ruined.
bankrupt.example: The company went bankrupt after several years of financial losses.

barren.simpleDefinition: (Of land) too poor to produce vegetation; (of a female animal or woman) unable to have children; unproductive or empty.
barren.example: The barren landscape stretched for miles, devoid of any trees or plants.

barrier.simpleDefinition: A fence or other obstacle that prevents movement or access; anything that prevents progress or communication.
barrier.example: Language can often be a barrier to effective communication between cultures.

barter.simpleDefinition: To exchange goods or services for other goods or services without using money.
barter.example: In ancient times, people would barter goods like salt for spices.

befuddled.simpleDefinition: Confused or perplexed, often by alcohol or a complex situation.
befuddled.example: The old man seemed befuddled by the sudden changes in technology.

belittle.simpleDefinition: To make someone or something seem unimportant or of less value.
belittle.example: It's never right to belittle someone's efforts, even if they fail.

belittlement.simpleDefinition: The act of making someone or something seem unimportant or of less value.
belittlement.example: Constant belittlement from his boss eroded his self-confidence.

bend.simpleDefinition: To force something straight into a curve or angle; to move your body downwards and forwards.
bend.example: You need to bend your knees slightly when lifting heavy objects.

biased.simpleDefinition: Showing an unfair preference for or against something or someone.
biased.example: The news report was criticized for being biased towards one political party.

bibliography.simpleDefinition: A list of books, articles, and other sources used when writing a research paper or book.
bibliography.example: The student included a comprehensive bibliography at the end of her thesis.

blaze.simpleDefinition: A very large or fiercely burning fire.
blaze.example: Firefighters quickly responded to the blaze that engulfed the old warehouse.

bleak.simpleDefinition: Lacking warmth, cheer, or hope; cold and miserable.
bleak.example: The future looked bleak for the company after the major financial loss.

blight.simpleDefinition: To spoil, harm, or destroy something, especially plants or a positive situation.
blight.example: A severe frost can blight an entire crop of fruit in one night.

boaster.simpleDefinition: A person who talks with excessive pride and self-satisfaction about their achievements or possessions.
boaster.example: Nobody likes to listen to a boaster who constantly talks about how great they are.

bohemian.simpleDefinition: Living an unconventional lifestyle, often associated with artists, writers, or musicians, with few permanent ties.
bohemian.example: She lived a bohemian life, traveling the world and creating art wherever she went.

bondage.simpleDefinition: The state of being a slave or being held captive; lack of freedom.
bondage.example: Many people fought for centuries to escape from the bondage of oppression.

boorishness.simpleDefinition: Rude, crude, or insensitive behavior; a lack of refinement or good manners.
boorishness.example: His boorishness at the dinner table offended all the guests.

braggart.simpleDefinition: A person who boasts about their achievements or possessions in an arrogant way.
braggart.example: The braggart couldn't stop telling everyone about his expensive new car.

braking.simpleDefinition: The act of slowing down or stopping a vehicle or machine using a brake.
braking.example: Smooth braking is essential for safe driving, especially in heavy traffic.

breakable.example: Please handle the package with care; it contains breakable items.

brittle.simpleDefinition: Hard but liable to break or shatter easily.
brittle.example: The old plastic had become brittle and cracked easily when touched.

broker.simpleDefinition: A person who buys and sells goods or assets for others, often for a commission.
broker.example: She hired a real estate broker to help her find a new apartment.

brooding.simpleDefinition: Deeply thoughtful and serious, often in a way that suggests sadness or worry.
brooding.example: He sat in the corner, a brooding expression on his face, lost in thought.

bucolic.simpleDefinition: Relating to the pleasant aspects of the countryside and country life.
bucolic.example: The painting depicted a peaceful bucolic scene with sheep grazing in a meadow.

build in.simpleDefinition: To include something as a permanent or integral part of a larger structure or system.
build in.example: The new software has a security feature built in to protect user data.

bureaucrat.simpleDefinition: An official in a government department or public institution, often seen as being concerned with official rules and procedures.
bureaucrat.example: Dealing with the city's bureaucrats can sometimes be a slow and frustrating process.

buried.simpleDefinition: Placed or hidden underground, or covered completely.
buried.example: The ancient treasure was buried deep beneath the old oak tree.

bustling.simpleDefinition: Full of activity, movement, and noise.
bustling.example: The market was bustling with shoppers preparing for the holiday season.

butter.simpleDefinition: A pale yellow edible fatty substance made by churning cream and used as a spread or in cooking.
butter.example: She spread butter generously on her toast every morning.

bygone.simpleDefinition: Belonging to an earlier time; past.
bygone.example: They often reminisced about the bygone days of their youth.

candour.simpleDefinition: The quality of being open, honest, and straightforward in speech or behavior.
candour.example: Her candour was refreshing; she always spoke her mind without hesitation.

cannibal.simpleDefinition: A person who eats the flesh of other human beings, or an animal that eats others of its own kind.
cannibal.example: In some animal species, a female may become a cannibal and eat her own young.

capacious.simpleDefinition: Having a lot of space inside; roomy.
capacious.example: The capacious backpack could hold all her camping gear for the week.

capitalist.simpleDefinition: A person who supports or practices capitalism, especially one who owns a lot of capital and uses it to generate wealth.
capitalist.example: As a successful capitalist, he invested his profits back into new businesses.

castigate.simpleDefinition: To criticize someone severely or punish them for something they have done wrong.
castigate.example: The coach had to castigate the team for their poor performance in the first half.

casual.simpleDefinition: Happening by chance, without planning, or not serious or formal.
casual.example: She made a casual remark about moving, but I think she was serious.

categorical.simpleDefinition: Absolutely and completely clear, without any doubt or conditions.
categorical.example: The manager gave a categorical denial of any wrongdoing.

celibacy.simpleDefinition: The state of abstaining from marriage and sexual relations, often for religious reasons.
celibacy.example: Many religious orders require their members to practice celibacy.

cereal.simpleDefinition: A grain used for food, such as wheat, oats, or rice, or a breakfast food made from these grains.
cereal.example: For breakfast, I usually have a bowl of cereal with milk.

chagrin.simpleDefinition: A feeling of strong annoyance, embarrassment, or disappointment, often caused by a failure or mistake.
chagrin.example: To her chagrin, she realized she had forgotten her wallet at home.

chastity.simpleDefinition: The state of being pure and virtuous, especially by refraining from sexual activity.
chastity.example: The knight swore an oath of chastity and loyalty.

chide.simpleDefinition: To speak to someone in a way that expresses mild disapproval or gentle criticism.
chide.example: She chided her son for leaving his toys all over the floor.

chronic.simpleDefinition: Lasting for a long time or constantly recurring, especially a disease or problem.
chronic.example: He suffers from chronic back pain that never seems to go away.

circulation.simpleDefinition: The movement of something, such as blood in the body, air, or money, or the number of copies of a newspaper or magazine distributed.
circulation.example: The newspaper has a daily circulation of over 100,000 copies.

cogitate.simpleDefinition: To think deeply and carefully about something; to ponder.
cogitate.example: He needed a quiet place to cogitate on the complex problem.

cogitating.simpleDefinition: Deep in thought; thinking carefully and deeply about something.
cogitating.example: She sat in her chair, a cogitating expression on her face.

coherent.simpleDefinition: Logical and consistent, making sense, or able to speak clearly and understandably.
coherent.example: The speaker presented a coherent argument that was easy to follow.

colossal.simpleDefinition: Extremely large or great in size, extent, or degree.
colossal.example: The company made a colossal profit last quarter.

come round.simpleDefinition: To regain consciousness after fainting, or to change one's opinion to agree with someone else's.
come round.example: After a few minutes, she started to come round and open her eyes.

commence.example: The ceremony will commence at exactly 10 o'clock.

commencement.simpleDefinition: The beginning or start of something, or a ceremony where degrees are awarded.
commencement.example: The commencement of the new project is scheduled for next month.

commend.simpleDefinition: To praise someone or something officially or publicly.
commend.example: The police officer was commended for his bravery.

communism.simpleDefinition: A political and economic system where all property is publicly owned, and each person works and is paid according to their abilities and needs.
communism.example: The theory of communism advocates for a classless society.

compassionate.simpleDefinition: Feeling or showing sympathy and concern for the suffering or misfortunes of others.
compassionate.example: The compassionate nurse comforted the worried patient.

compensate.simpleDefinition: To give someone something, typically money, in recognition of loss, suffering, or injury incurred; to make up for something.
compensate.example: The company had to compensate customers for the faulty product.

compile.simpleDefinition: To produce something, especially a list, book, or report, by assembling information collected from different sources.
compile.example: She spent hours compiling a list of potential clients.

complacency.simpleDefinition: A feeling of smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's achievements.
complacency.example: Their complacency led them to underestimate the competition.

complexity.simpleDefinition: The state of being complicated or intricate; the quality of having many interconnected parts.
complexity.example: The complexity of the legal case required many expert witnesses.

compliance.simpleDefinition: The act of obeying a rule, request, or law, or acting in accordance with an agreement.
compliance.example: The company must ensure full compliance with environmental regulations.

composite.simpleDefinition: Made up of several different parts or elements combined together.
composite.example: The new material is a composite of plastic and metal, making it both light and strong.

composure.simpleDefinition: The state of being calm and in control of your feelings, especially in a difficult situation.
composure.example: Despite the sudden emergency, she maintained her composure and quickly called for help.

conceal.simpleDefinition: To hide something or someone from view or from being known.
conceal.example: He tried to conceal his excitement, but a small smile gave him away.

conceited.simpleDefinition: Having an excessively high opinion of oneself or one's abilities.
conceited.example: Her conceited attitude made it difficult for others to work with her on the team.

conciliate.simpleDefinition: To stop someone from being angry or discontented; to pacify or make peace.
conciliate.example: The mediator tried to conciliate the two opposing parties to reach an agreement.

conclude.simpleDefinition: To bring something to an end; to finish. It can also mean to arrive at a judgment or opinion by reasoning.
conclude.example: After a long discussion, the committee decided to conclude the meeting and vote on the proposal next week.

concubine.simpleDefinition: A woman who lives with a man but has lower status than his wife or wives.
concubine.example: In ancient societies, it was not uncommon for powerful men to have concubines in addition to their legal wives.

condemn.simpleDefinition: To express strong disapproval of something; to officially declare something to be wrong or evil.
condemn.example: Many international organizations condemned the violence against innocent civilians.

condiment.simpleDefinition: A substance such as salt, mustard, or spice that is added to food to improve its flavor.
condiment.example: Ketchup and mustard are popular condiments served with hot dogs and hamburgers.

conducive.simpleDefinition: Making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible; helpful.
conducive.example: A quiet environment is conducive to studying and concentration.

conduit.simpleDefinition: A channel or pipe for conveying water or other fluids. It can also refer to a person or organization that acts as a channel for transmitting something.
conduit.example: The city installed a new underground conduit to improve the drainage system.

conflict.simpleDefinition: A serious disagreement or argument, often prolonged. It can also refer to a struggle or battle.
conflict.example: There was a clear conflict of interest when the judge ruled on a case involving his own company.

confound.simpleDefinition: To cause surprise or confusion in someone, especially by acting against their expectations.
confound.example: The sudden change in plans confounded everyone, leaving them unsure of what to do next.

conger.simpleDefinition: A large, predatory marine eel, often found in rocky areas of the Atlantic and Mediterranean.
conger.example: Divers spotted a large conger eel hiding among the rocks on the seabed.

conscript.simpleDefinition: To enroll someone compulsorily into military service.
conscript.example: During wartime, many young men were conscripted into the army.

consolidation.simpleDefinition: The process of combining several things into a single, more effective, or coherent whole.
consolidation.example: The consolidation of the two small companies resulted in a much larger and more competitive business.

conspire.simpleDefinition: To make secret plans jointly to commit an unlawful or harmful act.
conspire.example: The two rivals conspired to overthrow the current leader of the organization.

constraint.example: Budgetary constraints prevented the team from hiring additional staff.

contemplative.simpleDefinition: Expressing or involving prolonged thought; thoughtful and reflective.
contemplative.example: She spent a contemplative afternoon sitting by the lake, lost in her thoughts.

continuation.simpleDefinition: The action of carrying something on over time or the state of being carried on.
continuation.example: The author promised a continuation of the story in a new book next year.

contradict.simpleDefinition: To deny the truth of a statement, especially by asserting the opposite.
contradict.example: His actions often contradict his words, making it hard to trust him.

contrary.simpleDefinition: Opposite in nature, direction, or meaning.
contrary.example: Despite the forecast, the weather turned out to be quite contrary to what was predicted.

contrast.simpleDefinition: The state of being strikingly different from something else in close conjunction.
contrast.example: The stark contrast between the old and new buildings was quite noticeable.

contravene.simpleDefinition: To violate or go against a law, rule, or custom.
contravene.example: Building without a permit would contravene local planning regulations.

conventional.simpleDefinition: Based on or in accordance with what is generally done or believed; traditional.
conventional.example: She preferred a conventional approach to problem-solving rather than trying new, untested methods.

convicted.simpleDefinition: Found guilty of a crime by a court of law.
convicted.example: The jury found the suspect convicted of theft after reviewing all the evidence.

conviction.simpleDefinition: A strong belief or opinion; also, the act of proving someone guilty of a crime.
conviction.example: She spoke with great conviction about the importance of environmental protection.

convolution.simpleDefinition: A coil or twist, especially one of many; something complex and difficult to follow.
convolution.example: The plot of the novel was full of unexpected convolutions, making it hard to predict the ending.

correspond.simpleDefinition: To be in agreement or harmony; to communicate by exchanging letters or emails.
correspond.example: The numbers in the report do not correspond with the figures from the previous quarter.

corroborate.simpleDefinition: To confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding.
corroborate.example: The witness's testimony helped to corroborate the victim's account of the incident.

cosmopolitan.simpleDefinition: Familiar with and at ease in many different countries and cultures; having a worldwide scope.
cosmopolitan.example: The city's diverse population gives it a truly cosmopolitan atmosphere.

cosmos.simpleDefinition: The universe seen as a well-ordered whole.
cosmos.example: Scientists continue to explore the vastness and mysteries of the cosmos.

counterfeit.simpleDefinition: Made in exact imitation of something valuable or important with the intention to deceive or defraud.
counterfeit.example: The police seized a large shipment of counterfeit designer handbags.

covenant.simpleDefinition: A formal, solemn, and binding agreement or promise.
covenant.example: The two nations signed a covenant to maintain peace and mutual cooperation.

craft.simpleDefinition: An activity involving skill in making things by hand; skill or expertise, especially in a particular profession or trade.
craft.example: Her beautiful pottery demonstrated her exceptional craft and attention to detail.

crank.simpleDefinition: An eccentric person, especially one who holds strange beliefs or behaves oddly.
crank.example: He's a bit of a crank when it comes to his theories about alien life.

craven.example: The craven soldier deserted his post during the battle.

cretin.example: Only a cretin would believe such an obvious lie.

critique.simpleDefinition: A detailed analysis and assessment of something, especially a literary, artistic, or philosophical work.
critique.example: The art critic published a detailed critique of the new exhibition.

crone.simpleDefinition: An old woman who is thin and ugly, often used in a derogatory or dismissive way.
crone.example: The children were scared of the old crone who lived alone in the spooky house.

crook.simpleDefinition: A dishonest person or a criminal; also, a bend or curve in something.
crook.example: The police arrested the crook who had been stealing from local shops.

cud chew.simpleDefinition: To repeatedly chew food that has been regurgitated from the stomach, as done by ruminant animals; figuratively, to ponder or think deeply about something.
cud chew.example: After dinner, the cows would often cud chew peacefully in the field.

cunning.simpleDefinition: Having or showing skill in achieving one's ends by deceit or evasion; also, skillful or clever.
cunning.example: The cunning fox managed to steal the chickens without being seen.

cupid.simpleDefinition: The Roman god of love, often depicted as a winged boy with a bow and arrow.
cupid.example: According to myth, Cupid's arrows could make anyone fall deeply in love.

curious.simpleDefinition: Eager to know or learn something; also, strange or unusual.
curious.example: The curious child asked many questions about how the machine worked.

currency.simpleDefinition: A system of money in general use in a particular country; also, the state of being generally accepted or in use.
currency.example: The euro is the official currency in many European countries.

cursive.simpleDefinition: Written with the letters joined together in a flowing style.
cursive.example: She wrote a beautiful letter in elegant cursive handwriting.

curved.simpleDefinition: Having a rounded or bent shape rather than a straight line.
curved.example: The road curved gently around the side of the mountain.

cut and dried.simpleDefinition: Already decided and therefore not open to discussion; simple and straightforward.
cut and dried.example: The solution to the problem was not as cut and dried as they initially thought.

cynic.simpleDefinition: A person who believes that people are motivated purely by self-interest rather than acting for honorable or unselfish reasons.
cynic.example: The cynic always found fault with every new proposal, believing it was driven by hidden agendas.

darken.simpleDefinition: To make or become dark or darker.
darken.example: The heavy clouds began to darken the sky before the storm.

dead and buried.simpleDefinition: Completely finished, forgotten, or no longer relevant.
dead and buried.example: The old proposal for the new bridge is now dead and buried; they've chosen a different plan.

dealings.simpleDefinition: The way a person or organization behaves towards others in business or personal relationships.
dealings.example: His honest dealings with clients earned him a good reputation in the community.

dearth.simpleDefinition: A scarcity or lack of something.
dearth.example: There was a dearth of fresh water in the village after the long drought.

debonair.example: The actor played a debonair secret agent who always looked impeccable.

debris.simpleDefinition: Scattered pieces of waste or remains, especially after something has been destroyed.
debris.example: After the earthquake, the streets were covered in debris from collapsed buildings.

decay.simpleDefinition: To rot or decompose through the action of bacteria and fungi.
decay.example: Without proper preservation, organic materials will quickly decay.

deceit.simpleDefinition: The action or practice of deceiving someone by concealing or misrepresenting the truth.
deceit.example: The company was accused of deceit in its advertising claims.

deceived.simpleDefinition: To make someone believe something that is not true, often to gain an advantage.
deceived.example: She felt completely deceived when she found out he had been lying to her for months.

defame.simpleDefinition: To damage the good reputation of someone by saying or writing bad things about them.
defame.example: He threatened to sue the newspaper for trying to defame his character.

defensible.simpleDefinition: Able to be protected against attack or criticism; justifiable.
defensible.example: Her argument was well-researched and logically defensible.

deflect.simpleDefinition: To cause something to change direction, especially after hitting something.
deflect.example: The goalkeeper managed to deflect the ball away from the goal.

defy.simpleDefinition: To openly resist or refuse to obey.
defy.example: The small nation continued to defy the demands of the larger power.

deleterious.example: Smoking has many deleterious effects on health.

deliberately.example: He deliberately ignored her calls because he was angry.

delicate.example: The antique vase was so delicate that she handled it with extreme care.

delirious.simpleDefinition: In an extremely excited state, often due to illness or fever, causing confusion and incoherent speech.
delirious.example: After hours of high fever, the patient became delirious and started talking nonsense.

delusive.simpleDefinition: Giving a false or misleading impression.
delusive.example: He held a delusive belief that he could win the lottery without buying a ticket.

demagogue.simpleDefinition: A political leader who seeks support by appealing to popular desires and prejudices rather than by using rational argument.
demagogue.example: The demagogue stirred up the crowd with promises of easy solutions to complex problems.

demise.example: We were saddened to hear of the sudden demise of the beloved author.

demobilize.simpleDefinition: To release soldiers from military service and send them home.
demobilize.example: After the war ended, the government began to demobilize thousands of troops.

demolish.simpleDefinition: To completely destroy a building or other structure.
demolish.example: The old factory was demolished to make way for a new shopping center.

demonstrative.simpleDefinition: Openly emotional or expressive, especially of affection.
demonstrative.example: She was a very demonstrative person, always hugging her friends and family.

demur.simpleDefinition: To raise doubts or objections, or show reluctance.
demur.example: She demurred at the suggestion that she should work extra hours without pay.

denigrate.example: It's unfair to denigrate someone's efforts without understanding their challenges.

denigration.simpleDefinition: The act of saying negative and unfair things about someone or something to damage their reputation.
denigration.example: The politician faced denigration from his opponents during the election campaign.

deny.simpleDefinition: To state that something is not true, or to refuse to admit or accept something.
deny.example: She chose to deny the accusations, claiming she was innocent.

depart.simpleDefinition: To leave a place, especially to start a journey.
depart.example: The train is scheduled to depart from platform 5 at 10:00 AM.

deprecate.simpleDefinition: To express disapproval of something, or to make something seem unimportant.
deprecate.example: He tended to deprecate his own achievements, even when they were significant.

derrick.simpleDefinition: A type of crane used for lifting and moving heavy objects, often found on ships or oil rigs.
derrick.example: Workers used a large derrick to lift the heavy machinery onto the ship.

desert.simpleDefinition: To leave someone or something without help or support, especially when they need it.
desert.example: The soldiers were ordered not to desert their posts during the battle.

desolation.simpleDefinition: A state of complete emptiness or destruction, or a feeling of great sadness and loneliness.
desolation.example: After the fire, the forest was a scene of utter desolation.

despair.simpleDefinition: The complete loss or absence of hope.
despair.example: Faced with so many challenges, she felt a deep sense of despair.

destitute.simpleDefinition: Without money, food, a home, or possessions; extremely poor.
destitute.example: The war left thousands of people destitute and without shelter.

destruction.simpleDefinition: The act of causing so much damage to something that it no longer exists or cannot be repaired.
destruction.example: The earthquake caused widespread destruction across the city.

desultory.simpleDefinition: Lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; jumping from one thing to another without a clear focus.
desultory.example: He made a few desultory attempts to clean the room before giving up.

deter.simpleDefinition: To discourage someone from doing something, often by making them afraid or doubtful.
deter.example: The high fences were meant to deter intruders from entering the property.

devious.simpleDefinition: Using dishonest or indirect methods to achieve a goal, or not straightforward.
devious.example: He used devious tactics to get what he wanted, often misleading others.

devoid.simpleDefinition: Completely lacking in something important or essential.
devoid.example: The speech was devoid of any real substance or new ideas.

diagnosis.simpleDefinition: The process of identifying the nature of an illness or other problem by examining the symptoms.
diagnosis.example: The doctor's diagnosis confirmed that she had a common cold.

dictator.simpleDefinition: A ruler who has complete power over a country, typically one who has obtained control by force and allows no opposition.
dictator.example: The country suffered under the harsh rule of a military dictator for decades.

dilemma.simpleDefinition: A situation in which a difficult choice has to be made between two or more alternatives, especially equally undesirable ones.
dilemma.example: She faced a dilemma: either miss her friend's wedding or lose her job.

dilettante.simpleDefinition: A person who cultivates an area of interest, such as art or music, without real commitment or knowledge.
dilettante.example: He was a dilettante in painting, enjoying it as a hobby but never mastering it.

discarded.simpleDefinition: Thrown away or gotten rid of because it is no longer wanted or useful.
discarded.example: The children played with the discarded toys they found in the attic.

discontented.simpleDefinition: Not satisfied or happy with your situation or with things as they are.
discontented.example: The workers became increasingly discontented with their low wages and long hours.

discordant.simpleDefinition: Not in agreement or harmony; producing a harsh or unpleasant sound.
discordant.example: The discordant notes from the orchestra made the audience wince.

discover.simpleDefinition: To find something unexpectedly or in the course of a search, or to learn about something for the first time.
discover.example: Scientists hope to discover new planets capable of supporting life.

disgraceful.simpleDefinition: Very bad or unacceptable, causing shame or a loss of respect.
disgraceful.example: His behavior at the party was absolutely disgraceful.

disinterested.simpleDefinition: Not influenced by personal feelings, opinions, or advantages; impartial.
disinterested.example: A judge must remain disinterested to ensure a fair trial.

dismay.simpleDefinition: A feeling of shock and unhappiness, often caused by something unexpected.
dismay.example: To her dismay, the package she was expecting never arrived.

disparage.simpleDefinition: To speak about someone or something in a way that shows you do not respect them or that makes them seem less important.
disparage.example: It's unfair to disparage someone's efforts without understanding the challenges they faced.

disparity.simpleDefinition: A great difference between two or more things, especially an unfair difference.
disparity.example: The disparity in wealth between the rich and the poor continues to grow.

dispatch.simpleDefinition: To send someone or something quickly to a particular place for a specific purpose.
dispatch.example: The emergency services were dispatched to the scene of the accident immediately.

disperse.simpleDefinition: To spread out over a wide area, or to cause something to spread out.
disperse.example: The police used tear gas to disperse the crowd of protesters.

disputation.simpleDefinition: A formal argument or debate, especially one that is public or academic.
disputation.example: The scientific community engaged in a lengthy disputation over the new theory.

dissipate.simpleDefinition: To gradually disappear or cause something to disappear, or to waste money, time, or energy.
dissipate.example: The morning fog began to dissipate as the sun rose higher.

distasteful.simpleDefinition: Unpleasant or offensive, causing a feeling of dislike or disapproval.
distasteful.example: Many found his comments about the situation to be quite distasteful.

distract.simpleDefinition: To take someone's attention away from what they are doing or should be doing.
distract.example: Loud music can easily distract me when I'm trying to study.

distraught.simpleDefinition: So upset and worried that you cannot think clearly or behave normally.
distraught.example: She was distraught after losing her pet and couldn't stop crying.

divergence.simpleDefinition: The process or fact of separating and going in different directions, or of becoming different.
divergence.example: There was a clear divergence of opinion among the committee members on the new policy.

diversion.simpleDefinition: The act of changing the direction or use of something, or something that takes your attention away from serious matters.
diversion.example: The road closure caused a diversion, making our journey longer.

divine.simpleDefinition: Relating to or coming from God or a god, or extremely good or pleasing.
divine.example: Many ancient cultures believed in the divine power of nature.

doctrine.simpleDefinition: A belief or set of beliefs held and taught by a church, political party, or other group.
doctrine.example: The political party's doctrine emphasized individual liberty and free markets.

dotage.simpleDefinition: The period of life when a person is old and has become weak and confused.
dotage.example: In his dotage, he often forgot where he had put his keys.

drowsiness.simpleDefinition: A state of feeling sleepy and not fully awake.
drowsiness.example: The medication caused a feeling of drowsiness, so she avoided driving.

dubiousness.simpleDefinition: The state of being doubtful or questionable, or not entirely trustworthy.
dubiousness.example: The dubiousness of his claims made the jury question his testimony.

duffer.simpleDefinition: A person who is clumsy, incompetent, or stupid, especially at a particular activity.
duffer.example: He called himself a duffer at golf, always hitting the ball into the rough.

dullard.example: The teacher patiently explained the concept again for the dullard in the back row.

easygoing.simpleDefinition: Relaxed, tolerant, and not easily worried, annoyed, or upset.
easygoing.example: Her easygoing nature made her a popular friend and colleague.

eat drink and be merry.simpleDefinition: To enjoy oneself fully, especially without worrying about the future.
eat drink and be merry.example: After finishing the difficult project, they decided to eat, drink, and be merry for the evening.

eat into vitals.simpleDefinition: To gradually destroy or weaken something essential, or to cause deep and lasting damage.
eat into vitals.example: The constant stress began to eat into his vitals, affecting his health.

effeminacy.simpleDefinition: The quality in a man of having characteristics that are traditionally considered feminine.
effeminacy.example: Some critics unfairly associated his artistic style with effeminacy.

effusive.simpleDefinition: Expressing feelings of gratitude, pleasure, or approval in an unrestrained or heartfelt manner.
effusive.example: She gave an effusive thank-you speech after receiving the award.

egoistic.simpleDefinition: Excessively conceited or self-centered; concerned only with one's own interests.
egoistic.example: His egoistic attitude made it difficult for him to work well in a team.

elated.simpleDefinition: Extremely happy and excited, often because of a success or achievement.
elated.example: She was absolutely elated when she heard the news of her promotion.

elective.simpleDefinition: chosen by election or by choice; not required.
elective.example: Students can choose two elective courses in their final year.

electorate.simpleDefinition: all the people in a country or area who are allowed to vote in an election.
electorate.example: The electorate will decide the next leader in the upcoming election.

electrify.simpleDefinition: to make someone feel very excited or shocked; to supply with electricity.
electrify.example: The band's energetic performance truly electrified the crowd.

elegy.simpleDefinition: a sad poem or song, often written to express sorrow for someone who has died.
elegy.example: The poet wrote a beautiful elegy for his departed friend.

elevate.simpleDefinition: to raise something or someone to a higher position or level; to improve the quality or status of something.
elevate.example: The company decided to elevate her to a managerial position.

elocution.simpleDefinition: the skill of clear and expressive speech, especially in public speaking.
elocution.example: Her elocution was so perfect that every word she spoke was clear and impactful.

elusiveness.simpleDefinition: the quality of being difficult to find, catch, or achieve; the state of being hard to understand or remember.
elusiveness.example: The elusiveness of the suspect made the police investigation very challenging.

embezzlement.simpleDefinition: the act of secretly taking money that belongs to an organization or company where you work.
embezzlement.example: He was arrested for embezzlement after stealing funds from the charity.

emigrant.simpleDefinition: a person who leaves their own country to live permanently in another.
emigrant.example: Many emigrants sent money back to their families in their home country.

empirical.simpleDefinition: based on, concerned with, or verifiable by observation or experience rather than theory or pure logic.
empirical.example: The scientist relied on empirical data to support her conclusions.

emulation.simpleDefinition: the act of trying to be like someone or something else, often because you admire them.
emulation.example: Younger athletes often strive for emulation of their sports heroes.

enamoured.simpleDefinition: filled with a feeling of love for someone or a strong liking for something.
enamoured.example: He became completely enamoured with the beautiful scenery of the mountains.

encomium.simpleDefinition: a speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something highly.
encomium.example: The mayor delivered an encomium for the retiring police chief.

encumber.simpleDefinition: to make it difficult for someone to move or do something; to burden or hinder.
encumber.example: The heavy backpack encumbered her movements as she climbed the steep hill.

encyclopedia.simpleDefinition: a book or set of books giving information on many subjects or on many aspects of one subject, typically arranged alphabetically.
encyclopedia.example: She looked up the definition of the word in the encyclopedia.

endurable.simpleDefinition: able to be tolerated or borne; capable of being sustained.
endurable.example: The pain was endurable, but she still wished it would go away.

enduring.simpleDefinition: lasting over a long period of time; continuing to exist.
enduring.example: The novel's enduring popularity proves its timeless appeal.

enhance.simpleDefinition: to improve the quality, value, or extent of something.
enhance.example: Good lighting can greatly enhance the atmosphere of a room.

enlarge.simpleDefinition: to make something bigger or more extensive.
enlarge.example: They decided to enlarge their house by adding another room.

enormous.simpleDefinition: very large in size, quantity, or extent.
enormous.example: The company made an enormous profit last quarter.

entertain.simpleDefinition: to provide amusement or enjoyment for someone; to host guests.
entertain.example: They often entertain friends at their home on weekends.

enthralling.simpleDefinition: holding one's attention completely; fascinating and captivating.
enthralling.example: The documentary about ancient civilizations was absolutely enthralling.

entrepreneur.simpleDefinition: a person who starts a business, taking on financial risks in the hope of profit.
entrepreneur.example: She is a successful entrepreneur who launched several tech startups.

enunciate.simpleDefinition: to pronounce words clearly and distinctly; to express a theory or idea clearly.
enunciate.example: Please enunciate your words clearly so everyone can understand you.

epicurean.simpleDefinition: devoted to the pursuit of sensual pleasure, especially in fine food and drink.
epicurean.example: He lived an epicurean lifestyle, always seeking out the finest culinary experiences.

episodic.simpleDefinition: Happening or appearing at irregular intervals; not continuous.
episodic.example: Her memory loss was episodic, meaning she would forget things sometimes but not always.

epitaph.simpleDefinition: A short text written on a tombstone or monument in memory of a deceased person.
epitaph.example: The epitaph on the old soldier's grave read, 'A life well-lived, a duty well-done.'

epithet.simpleDefinition: A descriptive word or phrase expressing a quality or characteristic of the person or thing mentioned. It can be used positively or negatively.
epithet.example: 'The Great' was an epithet often used to describe powerful rulers in history.

epitome.simpleDefinition: A perfect example of a particular quality or type; a summary of a larger work.
epitome.example: With her kindness and intelligence, she was the epitome of a perfect leader.

equanimity.simpleDefinition: Calmness and composure, especially in a difficult situation.
equanimity.example: Despite the chaos around her, she maintained her equanimity and calmly solved the problem.

equilibrate.simpleDefinition: To bring into or be in a state of balance.
equilibrate.example: The engineer worked to equilibrate the forces acting on the bridge to ensure its stability.

equip.simpleDefinition: To provide someone or something with the necessary items for a particular purpose.
equip.example: Before the expedition, they needed to equip themselves with warm clothing and camping gear.

equitable.simpleDefinition: Fair and impartial; treating everyone equally.
equitable.example: The judge made an equitable decision, ensuring both parties felt heard and respected.

errant.simpleDefinition: Straying from the proper course or standards; behaving wrongly.
errant.example: The teacher disciplined the errant student for disrupting the class.

escape.simpleDefinition: To get away from a place or a dangerous or undesirable situation.
escape.example: The deer managed to escape the hunter by running deep into the forest.

espy.simpleDefinition: To catch sight of something, often something distant or hidden.
espy.example: From the top of the hill, we could espy the distant city lights twinkling in the darkness.

esteem.simpleDefinition: To regard someone with respect and admiration.
esteem.example: We esteem our elders for their wisdom and experience.

estimate.simpleDefinition: To roughly calculate or judge the value, number, quantity, or extent of something.
estimate.example: It's difficult to estimate the exact cost of the project without more detailed plans.

eternal.simpleDefinition: Lasting or existing forever; without end or beginning.
eternal.example: Many cultures believe in the concept of an eternal soul that lives on after death.

eulogistic.simpleDefinition: Expressing high praise or commendation, often in a formal speech or writing.
eulogistic.example: The eulogistic speech at the retirement party highlighted all of her achievements and contributions.

euphonious.simpleDefinition: Pleasing or sweet to the ear; having a pleasant sound.
euphonious.example: The poet chose euphonious words to create a beautiful and flowing verse.

evaluate.simpleDefinition: To assess the value, quality, importance, or condition of something.
evaluate.example: The committee will evaluate all the proposals before making a final decision.

evanescent.simpleDefinition: Soon passing out of sight, memory, or existence; quickly fading or disappearing.
evanescent.example: The beauty of the sunset was evanescent, fading quickly as night approached.

evasion.simpleDefinition: The act of avoiding something, especially something unpleasant or difficult.
evasion.example: His constant evasion of the question made it clear he was hiding something.

evenhanded.simpleDefinition: Treating all rivals or disputants equally; fair and impartial.
evenhanded.example: The referee was praised for his evenhanded approach to the game, making calls fairly for both teams.

evident.example: It was evident from her smile that she was happy with the news.

exaggeration.simpleDefinition: A statement that represents something as better or worse than it really is; overstating the truth.
exaggeration.example: His story about catching a fish 'as big as a car' was a clear exaggeration.

exaltation.simpleDefinition: The action of elevating someone or something in rank, power, or character; a feeling of extreme happiness or joy.
exaltation.example: The team felt a sense of exaltation after winning the championship.

excessive.simpleDefinition: More than is necessary, normal, or desirable; too much.
excessive.example: The doctor warned him that excessive sugar consumption could lead to health problems.

exclusion.simpleDefinition: The act of preventing someone or something from being included or participating.
exclusion.example: The club's policy led to the exclusion of several potential members.

exculpate.simpleDefinition: To declare someone not guilty of wrongdoing; to clear from blame.
exculpate.example: The new evidence helped to exculpate the suspect from all charges.

exempt.simpleDefinition: To free someone from an obligation or duty that others have.
exempt.example: Students with perfect attendance were exempt from the final exam.

exhausted.simpleDefinition: Extremely tired or completely used up.
exhausted.example: After running the marathon, the athlete felt completely exhausted.

exhort.simpleDefinition: To strongly encourage or urge someone to do something.
exhort.example: The coach exhorted his team to give their best effort in the second half.

exigency.simpleDefinition: An urgent need or demand; a situation requiring immediate attention.
exigency.example: The exigency of the situation required immediate action from the emergency services.

exorbitant.simpleDefinition: (Of a price or amount) unreasonably high or excessive.
exorbitant.example: The hotel charged an exorbitant price for a single night's stay.

expand.simpleDefinition: To become or make larger or more extensive.
expand.example: The company plans to expand its operations into new markets next year.

expel.simpleDefinition: To force someone to leave a place, especially a country or organization.
expel.example: The student was expelled from school for repeated violations of the rules.

exploration.simpleDefinition: The act of traveling in or through an unfamiliar area in order to learn about it.
exploration.example: The deep-sea exploration revealed many new species of marine life.

expose.simpleDefinition: To make something visible or known, especially something hidden or secret.
expose.example: The journalist worked to expose the corruption within the local government.

expound.simpleDefinition: To explain something in detail, often a theory or idea.
expound.example: The professor took time to expound on the complex philosophical concepts.

extempore.simpleDefinition: Spoken or done without preparation; impromptu.
extempore.example: She delivered an impressive extempore speech at the conference.

extradition.simpleDefinition: The official process by which a country sends a person accused or convicted of a crime to another country where the crime was committed.
extradition.example: The two nations signed a treaty to facilitate the extradition of criminals.

extravagance.simpleDefinition: The act of spending too much money or using too much of something; lack of restraint in spending.
extravagance.example: Her extravagance led her to buy designer clothes she didn't need.

extreme.simpleDefinition: Reaching the highest or greatest degree; very great.
extreme.example: The climbers faced extreme weather conditions on the mountain.

exult.simpleDefinition: To show great pleasure and excitement, especially after a victory or success.
exult.example: The fans exulted as their team scored the winning goal in the final minute.

facile.simpleDefinition: Appearing neat and comprehensive only by ignoring the true complexities of an issue; easily achieved but often superficial.
facile.example: The politician offered a facile solution to a very complicated economic problem.

facilitate.simpleDefinition: To make an action or process easier or less difficult.
facilitate.example: The new software will facilitate communication among team members.

faculty.simpleDefinition: An inherent mental or physical power; also, a department or group of teachers in a university.
faculty.example: She has a remarkable faculty for learning new languages quickly.

fade.simpleDefinition: To gradually grow faint, disappear, or lose color or brightness.
fade.example: The old photographs had started to fade over time.

famish.simpleDefinition: To suffer severely from hunger; to starve.
famish.example: After a long hike, they were famished and eager for a meal.

fanciful schemes.simpleDefinition: Plans or ideas that are imaginative and unrealistic, often impractical.
fanciful schemes.example: His business proposal was full of fanciful schemes that lacked any real financial backing.

fatalist.simpleDefinition: A person who believes that all events are predetermined and therefore inevitable, and that human beings are powerless to change them.
fatalist.example: As a fatalist, he accepted his misfortunes with a sense of resignation.

fathom.simpleDefinition: To understand a difficult problem or a mysterious person after much thought.
fathom.example: It was hard to fathom the true depth of her sadness.

feeble.simpleDefinition: Lacking physical strength, especially as a result of age or illness; weak.
feeble.example: The old man's voice was feeble, but his words were clear.

fiasco.simpleDefinition: A complete and embarrassing failure, especially of something planned.
fiasco.example: The elaborate plan to launch the new product turned into a complete fiasco when the main server crashed.

fiddling.simpleDefinition: Dealing with something in a trivial or unimportant way; also, making small, unnecessary adjustments.
fiddling.example: He spent hours fiddling with the settings on his phone instead of focusing on his urgent work.

finagle.simpleDefinition: To get something by using clever or dishonest methods.
finagle.example: She managed to finagle a free ticket to the concert by telling the organizer she was a journalist.

fire and brimstone.simpleDefinition: A phrase referring to the torments of hell, often used to describe a very angry or passionate speech about punishment.
fire and brimstone.example: The preacher delivered a fire and brimstone sermon, warning the congregation about the consequences of sin.

flagitious.example: The flagitious act of poisoning the community's water supply shocked everyone.

flashy.simpleDefinition: Attracting attention because of being bright, expensive, or showy, often in a way that lacks good taste.
flashy.example: He drove a flashy sports car that always turned heads wherever he went.

flat out.simpleDefinition: At maximum speed or effort; also, directly and without hesitation.
flat out.example: The athlete ran flat out for the entire race, determined to win.

flatten.simpleDefinition: To make something flat or flatter; to knock something down or defeat it completely.
flatten.example: The strong winds threatened to flatten the old wooden fence.

fleeting.simpleDefinition: Lasting for a very short time.
fleeting.example: They shared a fleeting moment of eye contact before looking away.

flexible.simpleDefinition: Able to bend or be bent easily without breaking; also, able to change or be changed easily according to the situation.
flexible.example: The company offers flexible working hours, allowing employees to choose their own schedule.

forecast.simpleDefinition: A statement about what is likely to happen in the future, especially concerning the weather or a financial trend.
forecast.example: The weather forecast predicts heavy rain for tomorrow afternoon.

formless.simpleDefinition: Without a definite or regular shape or structure.
formless.example: In the deep fog, the distant trees appeared as formless shadows.

forsaken.simpleDefinition: Abandoned or deserted; left alone and neglected.
forsaken.example: The old, crumbling house stood forsaken at the edge of the village.

fortuitous.simpleDefinition: Happening by chance, especially a lucky chance that brings a good result.
fortuitous.example: It was a fortuitous meeting that led to their successful business partnership.

fragile.example: The antique vase was so fragile that she handled it with extreme care.

fragrance.example: The fragrance of fresh roses filled the entire room.

frank.simpleDefinition: Open, honest, and direct in speech, sometimes in a way that might seem blunt.
frank.example: To be frank, I don't think that idea will work.

frantic.simpleDefinition: Wildly excited or anxious, especially because of worry or fear.
frantic.example: She made a frantic call to the police after realizing her child was missing.

freak.simpleDefinition: An unusual or unexpected event or thing; also, a person who is obsessed with a particular activity or interest.
freak.example: The sudden snowstorm in May was a complete freak of nature.

friction.simpleDefinition: Disagreement or conflict between people or groups; also, the resistance that one surface or object encounters when moving over another.
friction.example: There has been a lot of friction between the two departments recently.

frisky.example: The frisky puppy chased its tail around the living room.

frown.simpleDefinition: To wrinkle your forehead, usually because you are angry, worried, or thinking hard; also, to disapprove of something.
frown.example: The teacher frowned at the students who were talking during the lecture.

fruitful.simpleDefinition: Producing good or useful results; productive.
fruitful.example: Their collaboration proved to be very fruitful, leading to several new discoveries.

furtive.simpleDefinition: Done in a quiet and secretive way to avoid being noticed, often suggesting guilt or nervousness.
furtive.example: He cast a furtive glance at his watch, hoping no one would notice he was bored.

fussy.simpleDefinition: Easily worried or upset; also, paying too much attention to small, unimportant details.
fussy.example: She's very fussy about her food and won't eat anything she doesn't like.

gargantuan.simpleDefinition: Extremely large in size or amount.
gargantuan.example: The company built a gargantuan new factory that covered several acres.

generate.simpleDefinition: To produce or create something, especially energy or ideas.
generate.example: Wind turbines generate electricity from the power of the wind.

generous.simpleDefinition: Willing to give money, help, or time freely; larger than usual or necessary.
generous.example: She was very generous and donated a large sum to the local charity.

genesis.simpleDefinition: The origin or beginning of something.
genesis.example: The genesis of the idea came from a casual conversation between colleagues.

get along.simpleDefinition: To have a friendly relationship with someone; to manage or cope in a situation.
get along.example: Despite their different personalities, the two brothers always get along well.

gifted.simpleDefinition: Having exceptional natural ability or talent.
gifted.example: The gifted musician began playing complex pieces at a very young age.

glorious.simpleDefinition: Having great beauty or splendor; deserving great praise.
glorious.example: The sunset over the ocean was a truly glorious sight.

gloss.simpleDefinition: A shiny, smooth appearance on a surface.
gloss.example: The new car had a beautiful, high-gloss finish that reflected the light.

glow.simpleDefinition: To emit a soft, steady light; to show deep pleasure or health.
glow.example: Her face began to glow with happiness when she heard the good news.

goad.simpleDefinition: To provoke or annoy someone to stimulate an action or reaction.
goad.example: He tried to goad his sister into arguing with him, but she refused.

gourmand.simpleDefinition: A person who enjoys eating and often eats too much.
gourmand.example: The gourmand always ordered the largest portion on the menu and often asked for seconds.

gourmet.simpleDefinition: A person who has a refined taste in food and drink and enjoys high-quality cuisine.
gourmet.example: The gourmet traveled extensively to sample the finest dishes from around the world.

grain.simpleDefinition: The small, hard seed of a cereal plant, such as wheat or rice; a very small amount of something.
grain.example: Farmers harvest grain like corn and wheat to make bread and other foods.

grandiose.simpleDefinition: Impressive and magnificent in appearance or style, especially excessively so; intended to seem important or splendid.
grandiose.example: The architect presented a grandiose plan for a new city hall with towering spires and marble columns.

grant.simpleDefinition: A sum of money given by an organization, especially a government, for a particular purpose.
grant.example: The university received a research grant to study renewable energy sources.

grasp accurately.simpleDefinition: To understand something completely and correctly.
grasp accurately.example: It took him a while to grasp accurately the complex instructions for assembling the furniture.

grateful.simpleDefinition: Feeling or showing appreciation for something done or received.
grateful.example: She was truly grateful for all the help her friends offered during her difficult time.

gratifying.example: It was gratifying to see all her hard work finally pay off with such excellent results.

gratitude.simpleDefinition: The quality of being thankful; readiness to show appreciation for and to return kindness.
gratitude.example: He expressed his deep gratitude to everyone who supported him during the challenging project.

greeting.simpleDefinition: An act of welcome or acknowledgment upon meeting someone.
greeting.example: She offered a warm greeting to all the guests as they arrived at the party.

grueling.example: The marathon was a grueling race that tested the endurance of every runner.

haggler.simpleDefinition: A person who argues about the price of something in an attempt to get it at a lower cost.
haggler.example: The haggler spent an hour trying to get a better price for the antique vase at the market.

halcyon.simpleDefinition: Denoting a period of time in the past that was idyllically happy and peaceful.
halcyon.example: She often looked back fondly on the halcyon days of her childhood, free from worries.

hang in balance.simpleDefinition: To be in an uncertain or critical state, with the outcome not yet decided.
hang in balance.example: The future of the company hung in the balance after the unexpected financial losses.

harmonious.simpleDefinition: Forming a pleasing or consistent whole; free from disagreement or dissent.
harmonious.example: The choir sang in such a harmonious way that their voices blended perfectly.

harsh.simpleDefinition: Rough, severe, or unpleasantly grating to the senses or feelings.
harsh.example: The harsh winter wind made walking outside unbearable.

hastening.simpleDefinition: Moving, acting, or causing something to happen with great speed.
hastening.example: She was hastening along the path to catch the last bus home.

hasty.simpleDefinition: Done with excessive speed or without sufficient careful thought.
hasty.example: Making a hasty decision often leads to regret later on.

hazardous.simpleDefinition: Involving serious risk, danger, or peril to safety or health.
hazardous.example: Working with toxic chemicals can be extremely hazardous without protective gear.

head and ears.simpleDefinition: Completely, deeply, or thoroughly involved in something.
head and ears.example: He found himself head and ears in debt after starting the new venture.

heckle.simpleDefinition: To interrupt a public speaker with loud, rude, or aggressive comments.
heckle.example: A few angry protesters tried to heckle the mayor during his speech.

hedge.simpleDefinition: A boundary of bushes, or an action taken to protect against financial loss.
hedge.example: Investing in gold is often used as a hedge against inflation.

hefty.simpleDefinition: Large, heavy, powerfully built, or substantial in amount.
hefty.example: He had to pay a hefty fine for speeding through the school zone.

hegemony.simpleDefinition: Leadership or dominant influence exerted by one nation or social group over others.
hegemony.example: The ancient empire maintained its political hegemony over neighboring territories.

heinous.simpleDefinition: Utterly wicked, evil, shocking, or deserving of strong condemnation.
heinous.example: The criminal received a life sentence for committing such heinous acts.

hexagon.simpleDefinition: A flat geometric shape with six straight sides and six angles.
hexagon.example: Bees construct their honeycombs out of tiny, perfect hexagon cells.

hidebound.simpleDefinition: Unwilling to change or consider new ideas due to rigid tradition.
hidebound.example: The hidebound committee rejected every suggestion for modernizing the policy.

highbrow.simpleDefinition: Intellectual, scholarly, or appealing to refined and sophisticated tastes.
highbrow.example: He preferred reading highbrow historical essays over commercial magazines.

hindrance.simpleDefinition: A thing that provides resistance, delay, or obstruction to something.
hindrance.example: The lack of reliable internet was a major hindrance to her online studies.

hit upon.simpleDefinition: To discover, think of, or find something unexpectedly or by chance.
hit upon.example: After hours of brainstorming, the team finally hit upon a brilliant solution.

hoard.simpleDefinition: To accumulate and store away a large quantity of items secretly.
hoard.example: During the crisis, some merchants attempted to hoard essential food supplies.

hole and corner.simpleDefinition: Done secretly, underhandedly, or in a deceitful manner.
hole and corner.example: He refused to participate in such hole and corner business transactions.

holocaust.simpleDefinition: Destruction or slaughter on a mass scale, especially by fire or warfare.
holocaust.example: The devastating conflict resulted in a humanitarian holocaust for civilians.

homogeneous.simpleDefinition: Consisting of parts or elements that are all of the same kind; uniform.
homogeneous.example: The small island nation has a remarkably homogeneous culture and language.

honorary.simpleDefinition: Given as an honor or title without the normal duties or regular payment.
honorary.example: The university awarded him an honorary degree for his philanthropic work.

hook.simpleDefinition: A curved device used for catching or holding, or an attractive feature.
